rv.q: Flynn’s Cher is every inch the immaculate LA Barbie doll as Beverly Hills High School’s queen bee and self-appointed fashion guru. I lost count of the outfits that follow her tiny yellow tartan suit. Despite looking faintly appalled when dealing with lesser mortals, she manages to find Cher’s bottomless optimism.

But Cher’s own personal life slides off-kilter as she begins to realise that she has feelings for Josh, the son of her father’s ex-wife. Heckerling’s brisk, lightly nuanced screenplay makes a relatively stable and inventive transition to the stage.
Cher, like Jane Austen’s Emma Wodehouse upon whom she is playfully modelled, is “handsome, clever, and rich” with a penchant for matchmaking her peers – and yellow plaid miniskirts.

Emma Flynn is all smiles as the pampered, ditzy heroine Cher Horowitz; she has a strong voice too. And if any Austenites come to whoop it up in the audience, they will be pleased to see there is a programme note by an Oxford professor. It is mainly in terms of visuals that the show falls short.

What’s disappointing, certainly for the first half, is how little the songs add. The lyricist Glenn Slater is never less than adept in packing in the cheerfully time-locked teen speak; the composer KT Tunstall keeps everything chugging along very pleasantly, in a choppy, poppy style that wouldn’t alarm any Gen Xers in the stalls who had just wok...
Flynn works her knee-high socks off, but the social satire feels muted
Amy Heckerling adapts her own iconic screenplay for a lumbering production
Clueless can still stand up proudly in its overpriced stilettos
Emma Flynn is the breakthrough star of this production.
Clueless the musical has its moments, but it ultimately falls short of expectations.
